new_statements.quote: 1.5.4. Stress /ˊ/ This is characterised by – (i) a high pitch, (ii) a steep rise for the terminal, (iii) an ultra-length for the final vowel This occurs in emphasis and in vocatives. e.g. /laccimíi/ N.pr. fem. (voc.) … /itúuli/ 'a little' [p. 83] … Disyllabic words fall mainly under two categories in their relative prominence of constituent syllables. A. Prominence for the initial syllable that is 1-2 words with following pattern fall under this category. VVCV 1 2 aa-na 'elephant' … CVVCV … CVVCCV … CVVCVC [p. 85] B. Prominence more for the final syllable, that is 2-1. VCCVV 2 1 e-nnoo 'some where' … CVCV 2 1 pa-ti 'step' … CVCCV … CVVC(C)VV [pp. 86-88]
new_statements.citation: Indira, R. 1976. Descriptive analysis of Kāḍar. Ph.D. thesis, University of Poona (Centre of Advanced Study in Linguistics, Deccan College Postgraduate and Research Institute), Poona. Ch. 1 Phonology, secs. 1.5.4 'Stress' and 1.6.1.2-1.6.1.3 'Disyllabic words' / 'Trisyllabic words'.
new_statements.locator: pp. 83 (1.5.4 Stress), 85-88 (1.6.1.2 Disyllabic words), 88-90 (1.6.1.3 Trisyllabic words); PDF part-1 pages 56, 58-63
new_statements.rule_in_words: Indira separates two things. (a) 'Stress' proper (1.5.4) is a suprasegmental of emphasis and vocatives: high pitch, steep terminal rise and extra length on the final vowel (laccimíi!, caakkoó!, itúuli 'a little'). (b) Word-level prominence is described under the syllable (1.6.1.2-1.6.1.3) by ranking syllables 1 (most prominent), 2, 3. A long vowel attracts prominence: disyllables with a long first vowel (aa-na, paa-tti, kaa-yam, nii-lam) are initial-prominent (1-2); disyllables with a short first syllable (pa-ti, ka-ri, pa-tti, e-nnoo, e-ppoo) or with a long final vowel (aa-roo, aa-noo, vocative caa-kkoo, raa-yoo) are final-prominent (2-1). Trisyllables are medial-prominent when only the medial vowel is long (i-tuu-li 3 1 2, ka-too-la 2 1 3, ka-nnaa-ti) and initial-prominent when the first vowel is long (loo-laa-kke, pee-ti-ccu, caa-ti-kka, moo-ti-ram, kRaa-ppun-el 1 2 3). Provisional summary: prominence falls on the leftmost long-vowel syllable; in words with no long vowel (or with a long final vowel) it falls on the final syllable. Words of all short syllables (CVCVCV ka-ta-la, ka-yu-va) are listed without prominence numbers.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not named as such, but the 1/2/3 numbering ranks the remaining syllables (e.g. i-tuu-li 3 1 2 vs ka-too-la 2 1 3; loo-laa-kke 1 2 3), implying a secondary prominence on the second-ranked syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: The emphatic/vocative 'stress' (1.5.4) overrides word prominence: the final vowel of a vocative or emphasised word takes high pitch, terminal rise and ultra-length (/laccimíi/, /caakkoó/). Words with all short syllables (CVCVCV, quadrisyllables, pentasyllables) are given without prominence marks (pp. 90-92).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms (isolated words listed by syllable pattern). The 1.5.4 'stress' is an utterance-level feature of emphasis and vocatives, distinct from the word-prominence ranking. Data from the author's own fieldwork on Kāḍar (Poona thesis, 1976); scans are image-only, statement verified against the page images.
new_statements.identity_note: Indira 1976 describes 'Kāḍar' (the Kadar/Kada language of the Kerala hills, glottocode kada1242, not the Wayanad Kadars who speak Malayalam per Thundyil 1975: 229); the Shodhganga record's keywords name Chakkala and Karabara, Chakkala being one of the Kerala Kadar settlements listed by Thundyil, but the fieldwork site is not confirmed because the thesis introduction could not be re-fetched sources. Suresh 1981/82 covers the Anaimalai-hills (Tamil Nadu) Kadar. Glottolog's fourth reference (Sung 2013, a review of a book edited by Kádár) is a name-match error and is not about this language.

Sec. 1.5 Suprasegmentals (pp. 79-83) lists junctures, four pitch levels, terminals and 'Stress' /ˊ/ (1.5.4, p. 83) = high pitch + steep terminal rise + ultra-length of the final vowel, occurring 'in emphasis and in vocatives'. Sec. 1.6.1.2-1.6.1.3 (pp. 85-90) gives word-level 'relative prominence of constituent syllables' with numbered syllables: disyllables with a long initial vowel (VVCV, CVVCV, CVVCCV, CVVCVC) are initial-prominent (1-2); disyllables with a short initial syllable (CVCV, CVCCV, VCCVV) or a long final vowel (VVCVV aa-roo, CVVC(C)VV vocatives) are f…
No phonological description beyond the IPA of the name; further reading lists Ehrenfels 1952, Indira 1976, Thundyil 1978 'The Language and Culture of the Kadar', Suresh 1981.

sources.citation: Thundyil, Zacharias. 1975. The language of the Kadars. International Journal of Dravidian Linguistics 4(2): 229-248.
sources.note: PHONOLOGY (pp. 230-235) is a segmental inventory (vowels, consonants with examples) only; no mention of stress, accent, pitch or syllable prominence. Grammar and vocabulary follow.

sources.citation: Ehrenfels, U. R. 1952. Kadar of Cochin. Madras: University of Madras. Chap. XI 'The Kadan Language', pp. 257ff.
sources.note: Anthropological account; notes only sentence intonation ('beginning each sentence on a fairly high tone-level which is then gradually falling', p. 257) and slower speech tempo; treats the language as Kadan Tamil; no word-stress statement.
